title: Measurement, units and significant figures
note: Every measurement has some uncertainty, and the digits you report should show it. Significant figures are the certain digits plus one estimated digit. When multiplying or dividing, keep the fewest significant figures of any input; when adding or subtracting, keep the fewest decimal places.

read.title: What the digits are telling you
text: Suppose you weigh a coin on a balance that reads to the hundredth of a gram and see 2.53 g. The 2 and the 5 are certain, and the final 3 is your best estimate. All three are significant figures. Writing 2.530 g would claim a precision the balance never gave you, so the number of digits you record is a statement about the quality of the measurement.

Zeros need care. Zeros between nonzero digits always count. Zeros at the front of a small number, as in 0.0045, only locate the decimal point and never count. Trailing zeros after a decimal point do count, because someone chose to record them. Scientific notation removes doubt: 4.50 × 10³ clearly has three significant figures.

Calculated results cannot be more certain than the data behind them. For multiplication and division, the answer keeps as many significant figures as the input with the fewest. For addition and subtraction, what matters is decimal places: the answer stops at the last decimal place that every input shares. Counted quantities and defined conversions, such as 1000 mL in a liter, are exact and never limit an answer.
Finally, precise is not the same as accurate. Precise measurements agree with each other; accurate ones are close to the true value. A miscalibrated balance can be very precise and still wrong.

q.q: Why should a mass read as 2.53 g not be written as 2.530 g?
